Lab 7. Landscape metrics.

Quantifying landscape patterns.

Author

Travis Belote

Background

Landscape ecologists are often interested in patterns of ecosystems. Different processes give rise to different patterns, and different patterns can govern different processes. This reciprocal relationship between pattern and process led Pete McKinley (Senior Conservation Biologist with The Wilderness Society) to say, “pattern IS process”.

See historical photo of the patterns that fire created on the west side of Mission Mountains and the ways that forest managers sometimes attempt to harvest timber and reduce fuels mimicking these natural patterns. The historical image is from the Confederated Salish Kootenai’s Division of Fish, Wildlife, Recreation, and Conservation and can be found here.

When we talk about patterns, sometimes we’re talking about patterns in data (i.e., histogram or frequency distribution of values or a distinct relationship between variables in a scatterplot). In landscape ecology, we’re typically referring to geographic patterns. In other words, “pattern” in landscape ecology usually refers to the distinct arrangement of ecological objects - be it individual organisms (e.g., how trees or elk are distributed in a given area) or broader land cover classes (e.g., forest patches of various sizes in a given area).

Landscape ecologists have developed metrics for quantify what is often visually apparent. These metrics can be focused on three distinct but related levels: (1) landscape metrics that characterize the full landscape, (2) class metrics that evaluate different types of classes (land cover types) individually, and (3) patch metrics that evaluate individual patches, which are identified by the adjacency of pixels with the same type (i.e., three forest pixels that share a boundary would be classified as a forest patch and be assigned a unique identifier at this level).

Landscape metrics.

There are many landscape metrics, but they are often correlated with one another. Here, we will focus on 4 different landscape-scale metrics: the aggregation index, contagion, edge density, and landscape richness,

As a landscape metric, the aggregation index and contagion measure how clumped or dispersed like classes tend to be, which can also be correlated with edge density. Edge density can be assessed across the entire landscape or for individual classes (we will do both). Landscape diversity – in our case richness – measure how many different types are in an area. You can calculate other measures of diversity (Shannon-Wiener and evenness) too.

Class metrics.

Here, we will evaluate the percent of the landscape occupied by specific classes (e.g., evergreen forests), the number of patches, and an edge index (how much “edge” does a specific class possess).

Patch metrics

For patch metrics, we will only investigate patch size distributions, which is a count of the number of patches of different sizes (i.e., a histogram of patch sizes). Landscapes can be characterized by a few large patches or sometimes many small patches and have a class occupy the same total area.

Simulated landscapes

We will start by investigating these landscape metrics with simulated landscapes that I created using the NLMR package in R. The simulated landscapes were produced using a two-dimensional fractional Brownian motion landscape with five different fractal dimensions. These details are not important for our purposes here; I share them in case some are interested. Each of the five simulated landscape is composed of only two classes (we can think of them as forest and non-forest), has the same composition (i.e., 30% of the pixels are “forest”), but with different patterns. We explore the differences in these patterns.

Start by loading packages (install them if you need to), and bring in the simulated landscapes by reading the .tif files from the directory and stacking them with rast(). Plot the landscapes to see what they look like. Imagine that green is forest and grey is not forest.

library(terra)
terra 1.8.60

Landscape metrics

Let’s start off looking at the whole landscape with landscape metrics. This is a bit confusing because the package is called landscapemetrics. Recall that landscape metrics here are metrics that consider the entire landscape and not just a specific class or patch of class. We will focus on four landscape metrics described above: Aggregation index (lsm_l_ai), Contagion (lsm_l_contag), Edge density (lsm_l_ed), and Patch richness (lsm_l_pr) these can be calculated using the parenthetical functions in landscapemetrics.

# LANDSCAPE METRICS

# Let's calculate these for our stack of simulated rasters
# We can do this by calling up the landscape metric function and apply it 
# right to the stack
landscapemetrics::lsm_l_ai(sim_Stack)

Take a look at the output and compare the values (far left variable) for each simulated landscape (rows in the table). Notice that “class” and “id” have NA values. This is because these functions are focused on the entire landscape and not any particular class. These fields will be populated when we calculate class and patch metrics.

That was pretty easy, but we can efficiently calculate many metrics at once using calculate_lsm. We will list the functions we are interested in and name the list ls_metrics. Then use calculate_lsm on our stack of simulated landscapes (sim_Stack) and tell the function what we want to run, which in this case are the metrics we’ve listed in ls_metrics.

# landsacpemetrics allows you to calculate several of these at once.
# first we need to create a list of which functions we want to use
ls_metrics <- c("lsm_l_ai", "lsm_l_contag", "lsm_l_ed", "lsm_l_pr")

# then use "calculate_lsm" and apply it to our stack, using "what" to call the list we made
landscape_metrics <- calculate_lsm(sim_Stack, what = ls_metrics)

After we run that View() the output. You could use this output right in your paper or further analysis, but let’s use plots to be able to compare values more easily. We will put the different landscapes along the x-axis for easier comparisons and plot the metric on the y-axis. Because the different metrics are listed in our output, we can easily facet by these to compare multiple metrics in one multi-panel figure.

# Let's plot the results
landscape_metrics %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(layer), y = value)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free_y") +
  xlab("Simulated landscape") +
  ylab("Metric value") +
  theme_bw()

That’s pretty nice. Look over the results. Do they reveal the patterns you might expect after looking at the maps of the simulated landscapes? I don’t like how the metrics are labeled. Let’s not force our readers to decode our figures. We can make some labels and add it to the plots.

# We can improve the labels. Let's first create a code and name lookup table
ls_metric_names <- c(
  ai     = "Aggregation Index",
  contag = "Contagion",
  ed     = "Edge Density",
  pr     = "Patch Richness")

# Now, include that in your labels so that readers don't have to decode anything
# We'll also make more meaningful labels of the different simulated landscapes 
# in the scale_x_discrete labels
landscape_metrics %>%
  filter(level == "landscape") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(layer), y = value)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free_y",
             labeller = labeller(metric = ls_metric_names)) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("1" = "Lots of small", 
                              "2" = "",
                              "3" = "Mixed",
                              "4" = "",
                              "5" = "Very few large")) +
  xlab("Simulated landscape") + ylab("Metric value") +
  theme_bw()

Class metrics

Now, let’s focus on the metrics associated with one class. In this case, because we’re treating the green pixels from the maps as forest, we want to calculate metrics ONLY for forest. We will focus on the percent of the landscape that is forest (lsm_c_pland), edge density of forest (lsm_c_ed), patch density (lsm_c_pd), and number of patches (lsm_c_np). As before, let’s list out which metrics we want to calculate and do this all at once. We’ll go ahead and list the codes and names in an object called class_metric_names for plotting and as reference.

## CLASS METRICS

# We'll go ahead and make our label lookup table
class_metric_names <- c(
  pland  = "Percent of landscape",
  ed     = "Edge Density",
  pd     = "Patch density", 
  np     = "Number of patches")

# Which class (cl) metrics do you want to calculate? 
# We will go ahead and list these
cl_metrics <- c("lsm_c_pland", "lsm_c_ed", "lsm_c_pd", "lsm_c_np")

# and tell R to calculate these
class_metrics <- calculate_lsm(sim_Stack, what = cl_metrics)

Go ahead and View() the output we made (class_metrics), but let’s plot it as before. We’re going to label the x-axis so that we know what 1 through 5 mean. I’m going to call 1 the landscape with “Lots of small” patches and 5 the one with “Very few large” patches for our plots. We’re still just focused on forest class, so we want to filter to get only the rows where class == 2. These are the green pixels in our maps.

class_metrics %>% dplyr::filter(class == 2) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(layer), y = value)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free_y", 
             labeller = labeller(metric = class_metric_names)) +
  xlab("Simulated landscape") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("1" = "Lots of small", 
                              "2" = "",
                              "3" = "Mixed",
                              "4" = "",
                              "5" = "Very few large")) +
  ylab("Metric value") +
  theme_bw()

Patch metrics

Finally, let’s treat every patch of forest as its own object of interest. We’ll look at how the patch size distributions vary among the simulated landscapes. We’ve already named them by the number of patches above, but this will allow us to quantify what we can see in the maps.

To do this, we’re only going to look at patch area, which treats adjacent pixels of the same class as a patch and calculates their area. We’ll use this to investigate patch size distributions. In other words, how many patches occur in different size classes? Note: defining a “patch” in gridded data requires that you be mindful of whether corner-adjacent pixels with the same class belong in the same patch or not. This is often referred to in the literature as “Rook’s case” (i.e., only consider 4 pixels sharing a border) or “Queen’s case” (i.e., consider all 8 pixels sharing a border or a corner). The default in landscapemetrics is Queen’s casde, but be aware that results can be sensitive to these decisions. See figure below from this publication.

Run the patch metrics and plot the patch size distributions for “forests” (class == 2) for each landscape. We’ll also improve the labels of the plots.

# run the area patch metrics
# note: you can change from Queen's case to Rook's case by adding directions = 4
# like this pa <- lsm_p_area(sim_Stack, directions = 4)
pa <- lsm_p_area(sim_Stack)

pa %>% dplyr::filter(class == 2) %>% ggplot(aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = "darkgreen") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~layer, scales = "free_x") + 
  xlab("Patch size") + ylab("Number") +
  theme_bw()
# Let's add labels to the facets so there's no guessing!
# Make the labels
landscape_labels <- c("1" = "Lots of small",
                      "2" = "Mostly small",
                      "3" = "Mixed",
                      "4" = "Few large",
                      "5" = "Very few large")

# Add the labels
pa %>% dplyr::filter(class == 2) %>% ggplot(aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = "darkgreen") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~layer, scales = "free_x", labeller = labeller(layer = landscape_labels)) + 
  xlab("Patch size") + ylab("Number") +
  theme_bw()

All five maps maintain the same amount of natural areas (30%). Along with your figures, write up a short paragraph describing your prediction and rationale.

OR

Re-run the code above but use Rook’s case (4-cell rule) to evaluate patch size distributions. How do the metrics change? Real Montana landscapes.

Let’s redo this analysis, but using real landscapes in Montana.

We will bring in the National Land Cover Database (NLCD) for 4 different places in Montana, visualize the data making sure to use the NLCD names and colors, calculate metrics of landscapes, classes, and patches, and compare these metrics among the landscapes.

First, bring in the boundaries of the landscapes and look at the aerial imagery under each. Don’t forget to use Google Earth or other aerial imagery as you interpret your data, develop hypotheses, and think about nature at landscape scales. Aerial imagery inspired Carl Troll to first coin the term “landscape ecology”, so don’t be shy about looking at photos of the Earth from space!

# Bring in 4 landscapes in Montana and look at them
real_landscapes <- vect("C:/Users/travi/TWS Dropbox/Travis Belote/BIOE515_LandEcol_Man_Fall2025/Labs/Lab 7/scratch/nlcd_samples.shp")
Warning: [vect] Z coordinates ignored
mapviewOptions(basemaps = "Esri.WorldImagery")
mapview(real_landscapes, col.regions = NA, alpha.regions = 0, color = "white", lwd = 2)

What do you notice about the natural patterns of these different landscapes? How much forest, shrub or grasslands, developed areas are there?

Now, let’s bring in the NLCD data, use a nice function to color-code the pixels per NLCD’s convention, and look at the landscapes.

# Bring in the land cover data for these landscapes 
treasurNLCD2 <- rast("C:/Users/travi/TWS Dropbox/Travis Belote/BIOE515_LandEcol_Man_Fall2025/Labs/Lab 7/scratch/real_landscapes/treasurNLCD.tif")
bobmarsNLCD2 <- rast("C:/Users/travi/TWS Dropbox/Travis Belote/BIOE515_LandEcol_Man_Fall2025/Labs/Lab 7/scratch/real_landscapes/bobmarsNLCD.tif")
bozemanNLCD2 <- rast("C:/Users/travi/TWS Dropbox/Travis Belote/BIOE515_LandEcol_Man_Fall2025/Labs/Lab 7/scratch/real_landscapes/bozemanNLCD.tif")
kootenaNLCD2 <- rast("C:/Users/travi/TWS Dropbox/Travis Belote/BIOE515_LandEcol_Man_Fall2025/Labs/Lab 7/scratch/real_landscapes/kootenaNLCD.tif")

# These steps assign the values in the raster to the codes and colors in the NLCD data
nlcd_classes <- data.frame(
  value = c(11, 21, 22, 23, 24, 31, 41, 42, 43, 52, 71, 81, 82, 90, 95),
  class = c("Open Water", "Developed Open Space", "Developed Low Intensity",
            "Developed Medium Intensity", "Developed High Intensity", "Barren Land",            "Deciduous Forest", "Evergreen Forest", "Mixed Forest",
            "Shrub/Scrub", "Grassland/Herbaceous", "Pasture/Hay",
            "Cultivated Crops", "Woody Wetlands", "Emergent Herbaceous Wetlands"))
levels(treasurNLCD2) <- nlcd_classes
coltab(treasurNLCD2) <- with(FedData::nlcd_colors(), data.frame(value = ID, R = col2rgb(Color)[1,], G = col2rgb(Color)[2,], B = col2rgb(Color)[3,]))

levels(bobmarsNLCD2) <- nlcd_classes
coltab(bobmarsNLCD2) <- with(FedData::nlcd_colors(), data.frame(value = ID, R = col2rgb(Color)[1,], G = col2rgb(Color)[2,], B = col2rgb(Color)[3,]))

levels(bozemanNLCD2) <- nlcd_classes
coltab(bozemanNLCD2) <- with(FedData::nlcd_colors(), data.frame(value = ID, R = col2rgb(Color)[1,], G = col2rgb(Color)[2,], B = col2rgb(Color)[3,]))

levels(kootenaNLCD2) <- nlcd_classes
coltab(kootenaNLCD2) <- with(FedData::nlcd_colors(), data.frame(value = ID, R = col2rgb(Color)[1,], G = col2rgb(Color)[2,], B = col2rgb(Color)[3,]))


# Look at the differences in landscape patterns. 
# Before you work on quantifying landscape metrics, it is a good idea to 
# view the patterns and consider the sizes of patches, their distributions,
# arrangements, etc. What do you notice in these locations?
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(treasurNLCD2, legend = F)
plot(bozemanNLCD2, legend = F)
plot(kootenaNLCD2, legend = F)
plot(bobmarsNLCD2, legend = F)

Now, let’s calculate the landscape, class, and patch metrics.

Landscape metrics

# Let's use the same metrics as above
ls_metrics <- c("lsm_l_ai", "lsm_l_contag", "lsm_l_ed", "lsm_l_pr")
cl_metrics <- c("lsm_c_pland", "lsm_c_ed", "lsm_c_pd", "lsm_c_np")
pa_metrics <- lsm_p_area

# We could create a list and do this in a loop, but let's do this one at a time.
treasur_ls <- calculate_lsm(treasurNLCD2, what = ls_metrics)
bozeman_ls <- calculate_lsm(bozemanNLCD2, what = ls_metrics)
kootena_ls <- calculate_lsm(kootenaNLCD2, what = ls_metrics)
bobmars_ls <- calculate_lsm(bobmarsNLCD2, what = ls_metrics)

Look at any of the outputs we made from above. Notice there’s no variable that allows us to differentiate between the real landscapes let’s add the names to each of the output tables from above # by creating a new variable with $landscape and assign the correct name to that variable.

treasur_ls$landscape <- "Treasure"
bozeman_ls$landscape <- "Bozeman"
kootena_ls$landscape <- "Kootenai"
bobmars_ls$landscape <- "Bob_Marshall"

# Now look at any of these
treasur_ls

Now, let’s combine these four landscapes into one dataframe using rbind (row bind).

lsm_real <- rbind(treasur_ls, bozeman_ls, kootena_ls, bobmars_ls)

And, let’s plot the patterns, going through a few options.

# and plot the data

# Let's flip the x and y to see how that looks
lsm_real %>% ggplot(aes(x = value, y = landscape)) +

# remember we made this label look-up table. Let's use it. 
ls_metric_names <- c(

  contag = "Contagion",
  ed     = "Edge Density",
  pr     = "Patch Richness")

# we'll add it to the plot and make the grey a little lighter
lsm_real %>% ggplot(aes(x = value, y = landscape)) +

Class metrics

Now, let’s calculate some class metrics.

###### Class metrics
# Let's use the same metrics as above
cl_metrics <- c("lsm_c_pland", "lsm_c_ed", "lsm_c_pd", "lsm_c_np")

# We could create a list and do this in a loop, but let's do this one at a time.
treasur_cl <- calculate_lsm(treasurNLCD2, what = cl_metrics)
bozeman_cl <- calculate_lsm(bozemanNLCD2, what = cl_metrics)
kootena_cl <- calculate_lsm(kootenaNLCD2, what = cl_metrics)
bobmars_cl <- calculate_lsm(bobmarsNLCD2, what = cl_metrics)

treasur_cl$landscape <- "Treasure"
bozeman_cl$landscape <- "Bozeman"
kootena_cl$landscape <- "Kootenai"
bobmars_cl$landscape <- "Bob_Marshall"

class_lsm_real <- rbind(treasur_cl, bozeman_cl, kootena_cl, bobmars_cl)
View(class_lsm_real)

Patch metrics

Finally, let’s look at patch metrics (patch size distributions) for Evergreen forests using the same steps but different functions as above.

###### Patch metrics
# Since we're only going to be looking at patch size distributions we'll just use this
# function

treasur_pa <- lsm_p_area(treasurNLCD2)
bozeman_pa <- lsm_p_area(bozemanNLCD2)
kootena_pa <- lsm_p_area(kootenaNLCD2)
bobmars_pa <- lsm_p_area(bobmarsNLCD2)

treasur_pa$landscape <- "Treasure"
bozeman_pa$landscape <- "Bozeman"
kootena_pa$landscape <- "Kootenai"
bobmars_pa$landscape <- "Bob_Marshall"

# use rbind to combine the output tables
patch_lsm_real <- rbind(treasur_pa, bozeman_pa, kootena_pa, bobmars_pa)
# look at it the data, notice "id"
View(patch_lsm_real)

# let's look at how the patch size distributions of evergreen forests vary
# among our landscapes
patch_lsm_real %>% dplyr::filter(class == 42) %>% ggplot(aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = "darkgreen") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~landscape) + 
  xlab("Patch size (hectares)") + ylab("Number") +
  theme_bw()
